questions.stem: "LIFO" means:
options: the last item pushed is the first one popped
the first item pushed is the first one popped
items are popped in sorted order
questions.explanation: First in, first out (b) is a queue — Week 7.

questions.stem: push(1), push(2), push(3), pop(), push(4), pop(). What does the next pop() return?
questions.explanation: The stack goes [1, 2, 3] → pop 3 → [1, 2] → push 4 → [1, 2, 4] → pop 4 → [1, 2]; the next pop returns 2.

questions.stem: A stack built on a dynamic array should keep its top at:
options: the end — the last used slot
questions.explanation: append and pop() at the end move nothing. Index 0 (a) shifts everything on every operation.

questions.stem: A stack built on a singly linked list should keep its top at:
questions.explanation: push_front and pop_front are O(1). At the last node (a), popping would need the node before it — an O(n) walk.

questions.stem: Stack().pop() on an empty stack:
questions.explanation: The contract says IndexError, as list.pop() does. Returning None (b) lets an error travel silently.

questions.stem: A stack on an array with its top at index 0. push costs:
questions.explanation: Inserting at index 0 of an array shifts every element — the "dishonest" design that still passes every test.

questions.stem: Why is "([)]" not balanced?
options: It has an odd number of brackets
) arrives when the most recent opener is [
The stack is not empty at the end
A closer arrives when the stack is empty
questions.explanation: The partner check fails. The count is even (a), and the stack is not empty at that point (d).

questions.stem: Which check makes is_balanced(")") return False?
options: a closer arrives when the stack is empty
questions.explanation: The closer finds nothing to match. The partner check (a) cannot even run.

questions.stem: The postfix form of 3 + 4 * 2 is:
questions.explanation: * binds tighter, so 4 2 * is computed first, then added to 3.

questions.stem: The postfix form of ( 3 + 4 ) * 2 is:
questions.explanation: The parentheses group 3 4 + first; the result is then multiplied by 2.

questions.stem: Evaluating the postfix 8 3 - gives:
questions.explanation: The first value popped (3) is the right operand, the second (8) the left: 8 − 3.

questions.stem: Evaluating the postfix 2 3 4 * + gives:
questions.explanation: 3 4 * is 12, then 2 12 + is 14.

questions.stem: In the shunting-yard algorithm, when an operator arrives, it first pops to the output every stacked operator with:
questions.explanation: Higher or equal. Strictly higher (d) is the rule for right-associative operators such as **.

questions.stem: Why does an operator of equal precedence also leave the stack?
options: So that - and / are left associative: 8 - 3 - 2 is (8 - 3) - 2
It makes no difference to the result
questions.explanation: Popping the earlier - before pushing the later one computes the left subtraction first.

questions.stem: The postfix form of 8 - 3 - 2 is:
questions.explanation: Left associative: (8 - 3) - 2. 8 3 2 - - (a) is 8 - (3 - 2), which is 7, not 3.

questions.stem: The worst-case extra space of is_balanced on a text of length n is:
questions.explanation: A text of n openers, ((((…, pushes all n.

questions.stem: To turn a recursive algorithm into a loop, in general you need:
options: nothing — every recursion is already a loop
questions.explanation: The call stack does the bookkeeping for a recursion; without it, you keep that stack yourself.

questions.stem: In an undo/redo system with two stacks, what happens to the redo stack when the user performs a new action?
options: the new action is pushed on it
questions.explanation: Redo only makes sense for actions just undone; a new action starts a new history.

questions.stem: n pushes onto the Stack of dsa/stack.py (built on a DynamicArray) cost in total:
questions.explanation: Each push is an append to the DynamicArray: amortised O(1).

questions.stem: Which of these is not a natural stack application?
options: serving customers in the order they arrived
questions.explanation: First come, first served is FIFO — a queue.

questions.stem: While is_balanced("(((())))") runs, the largest number of items on the stack at once is:
questions.explanation: Four openers in a row, then four closers.

questions.stem: peek() differs from pop() in that it:
options: returns the top without removing it
questions.explanation: And, like pop, it raises IndexError on an empty stack — so (d) is wrong.

questions.stem: The shunting-yard algorithm converts 2 * 3 + 4 to:
questions.explanation: * is stacked first; when + arrives, * has higher precedence and leaves first, so 2 3 * comes before 4 +. (a) is 2 * (3 + 4), and (c) and (d) are not postfix.

questions.stem: The shunting-yard algorithm converts ( 1 + 2 ) * ( 3 - 4 ) / 5 to:
questions.explanation: When / arrives, * is on the stack with equal precedence, so it leaves first: … * 5 /, which is ((1 + 2) * (3 - 4)) / 5. (a) is what the > bug produces: / waits on top of *, which computes (1 + 2) * ((3 - 4) / 5).

questions.stem: A student's infix_to_postfix pops an operator only when the stacked one has strictly higher precedence (> instead of >=). Their calculator, evaluate_postfix(infix_to_postfix(...)), now gives 8 - 3 - 2 as:
questions.explanation: The second - does not pop the first, so the postfix is 8 3 2 - -, which is 8 - (3 - 2) = 7. The right answer (a) is 3. No error (c): the postfix is well formed, just wrong.

questions.stem: With the same > bug, which of these inputs is still converted correctly?
questions.explanation: When * arrives, + is lower, so it stays under both rules; the two rules differ only for equal precedence. (b), (c) and (d) each have two operators of equal precedence in a row: (c) becomes 8 / (4 / 2) = 4.0 instead of 1.0, (d) 6 - (2 + 1) = 3 instead of 5.

questions.stem: evaluate_postfix(["6", "2", "/", "3", "*"]) returns:
questions.explanation: 6 / 2 is 3.0 (true division gives a float), then 3.0 * 3 is 9.0. (a) multiplies first, which the postfix order does not allow; exactly one value is left at the end, so there is no ValueError (d).

questions.stem: A buggy evaluate_postfix computes (first value popped) op (second value popped): the operands the wrong way round. On which input does it still give the right answer?
questions.explanation: Only + and * appear, and both commute, so the swapped order cannot show. (a) gives −5 instead of 5, (b) 0.33 instead of 3.0, (c) −2 instead of 2: every - and / exposes the bug, which is why the tests need them.

questions.stem: evaluate_postfix(["3", "4"]):
options: raises ValueError: two values are left at the end
questions.explanation: Two numbers and no operator leave two values on the stack; the contract says exactly one must remain, so the input is malformed. Returning the top (a) would hide the error.

questions.stem: evaluate_postfix(["1", "0", "/"]):
questions.explanation: The expression is well formed, so it is not a ValueError (b). Python's own 1 / 0 raises ZeroDivisionError, and evaluate_postfix lets it through.

questions.stem: A version of is_balanced ends with return True instead of return openers.is_empty(). Which input does it get wrong?
questions.explanation: ((a) leaves one ( on the stack, which only the empty-at-the-end check catches. The partner check still catches (a), and the non-empty check still catches (b) and (c), whose closer arrives on an empty stack.

questions.stem: A version of is_balanced pops for every closer without first checking that the stack is non-empty. On "())" it:
questions.explanation: After () the stack is empty; the second ) calls pop, and your Stack.pop raises IndexError: a crash instead of the answer False (b).

questions.stem: is_balanced("a(b)c)d(") returns False. Which check fails first?
options: a closer arrives when the stack is empty
questions.explanation: ( is pushed and matched by the first ); the second ) finds the stack empty, and the function returns False there. The final ( (c) is never reached.

questions.stem: is_balanced("print('(')"), a line of valid Python, returns:
options: True: the characters inside quotes are skipped
it raises an error on the quote characters
False: the ( inside the quotes is counted like any other
questions.explanation: is_balanced knows nothing about strings: it sees (, (, ), and one ( is left at the end. The counts are 2 and 1, not equal (b). A real parser first splits the text into tokens, so a bracket inside a string is not a bracket (Week 15).

questions.stem: Most pushes onto the Stack of dsa/stack.py are instant, but now and then one push takes much longer. Why?
options: The DynamicArray was full, so that push copies every item into a bigger block: O(n) for that push, amortised O(1) overall
The top is kept at index 0, so that push shifts every item
push walks to the end of the stack first
Python checks the whole stack for duplicates
questions.explanation: That is the resize of Week 4: rare, expensive pushes, paid for by the many cheap ones. The course stack keeps the top at the end, not at index 0 (b), and nothing walks (c).

questions.stem: Which stack gives worst-case O(1) for every push, not just amortised O(1)?
options: an array with the top at the end
an array with the top at index 0
a singly linked list with the top at the head
a singly linked list with the top at the last node
questions.explanation: push_front makes one node and moves one reference, always. The array with the top at the end (a) is amortised O(1): a push that triggers a resize copies everything. (b) and (d) are O(n) designs.

questions.stem: s = Stack([1, 2, 3]). What does s.pop() return?
questions.explanation: Stack(values) pushes the values in order, so the last one, 3, is the top. A stack built from values is not empty (d).

questions.stem: Two peek() calls in a row, with nothing in between, return two different values. The most likely bug is that peek:
options: reads index 0 instead of the last slot
forgets to raise IndexError on an empty stack
questions.explanation: A peek that removes is a pop: the second call sees the item underneath. Reading index 0 (a) is wrong too, but it would return the same wrong value twice.

questions.stem: An editor with an undo stack and a redo stack. The user types A, types B, types C, then: undo, undo, redo, types D. What is on the two stacks (bottom → top)?
options: undo: A B D · redo: empty
undo: A B C D · redo: empty
undo: A B D · redo: C
undo: A D · redo: C B
questions.explanation: Undo, undo: C, then B, move to the redo stack. Redo moves B back. Typing D pushes D on the undo stack and clears the redo stack, so C is gone (c). (b) forgets that C was undone.

questions.stem: nested_sum with your own Stack instead of recursion. Its real advantage in Python is that:
options: it adds the numbers in a different order, so the sum is more exact
a deeply nested input cannot raise RecursionError: your Stack has no 1,000-frame limit
questions.explanation: Both versions visit every item once, O(n) either way (a), and the explicit stack needs memory too (d). The gain is the depth limit: Python stops a recursion at about 1,000 frames, and does not optimise tail calls.

essays.stem: State the Stack ADT with the cost of each operation. Describe two honest implementations, compare them, and describe one design that passes every test but is not honest.
essays.answer:
• ADT: push(x), pop(), peek(), is_empty(), len() — LIFO, all O(1); pop and peek raise IndexError when empty.
  • On a dynamic array, top at the end: push is amortised O(1) (occasional resize), pop and peek O(1); compact memory, contiguous.
  • On a linked list, top at the head: all worst-case O(1); a node per item (about six times the memory of an array slot).
  • Dishonest: top at index 0 of an array — every push and pop shifts all the elements, O(n) each, O(n2) for n operations — yet the stack behaves correctly and passes every test.

essays.stem: Describe the stack algorithm for balanced brackets. Give an example of each of the three ways a text can be unbalanced, and the check that catches it.
essays.answer:
• Scan the text. Opener: push. Closer: the stack must be non-empty and the popped opener must be its partner. End: the stack must be empty. Other characters are ignored.
  • Wrong partner: ([)] — ) pops [.
  • Closer with nothing open: ) or ()) — the stack is empty when a closer arrives.
  • Opener never closed: ( or (() — the stack is not empty at the end.
  • O(n) time, O(n) space in the worst case.

essays.stem: Explain how a stack evaluates a postfix expression. Why does the order in which the two operands are popped matter, and for which operators?
essays.answer:
• Scan the tokens: push numbers; for an operator, pop two values, apply it, push the result; at the end exactly one value must remain (otherwise the input was malformed).
  • The first value popped is the right operand and the second the left, because the left operand was pushed earlier.
  • It matters for the non-commutative operators, - and /: 8 3 - must be 8 − 3 = 5, not 3 − 8 = −5.

essays.stem: Explain the shunting-yard algorithm, and trace it on 2 * ( 3 + 4 ) - 5. Why must an operator of equal precedence be popped?
essays.answer:
• Output list and operator stack. Numbers go to the output; ( is pushed; ) pops to the output down to the matching (; an operator pops every stacked operator of higher or equal precedence, then is pushed; at the end the stack is emptied to the output.
  • Trace of 2 * ( 3 + 4 ) - 5:
TokenOutputStack
22
*2*
(2* (
32 3* (
+2 3* ( +
42 3 4* ( +
)2 3 4 +*
-2 3 4 + *-
52 3 4 + * 5-
end2 3 4 + * 5 -
  • Equal precedence pops so that left-associative operators apply left to right: in 8 - 3 - 2, the first - must be applied before the second.

essays.stem: "Recursion is a stack." Explain, and describe how you would rewrite a recursive algorithm without recursion. When is that worth doing in Python?
essays.answer:
• Every call pushes a frame (its local variables and where to return) on the call stack, and every return pops one — so a recursion is a computation driven by a stack.
  • Rewrite: push the initial problem on an explicit Stack; loop while it is not empty: pop a problem, solve it directly if it is a base case, otherwise push its sub-problems.
  • Worth it in Python when the recursion could go deeper than about 1,000 frames (RecursionError), since there is no tail-call optimisation — e.g. a depth-first search on a large graph (Week 14).

essays.stem: A student's infix_to_postfix pops an operator only on strictly higher precedence (> instead of >=). Give one input that it still converts correctly and one that it gets wrong, with both postfix results and their values. Explain why the tests can miss this bug, and name an operator for which > is the right rule.
essays.answer:
• Still right: 3 + 4 * 2. It gives 3 4 2 * + = 11 under both rules: when * arrives, + is lower, and the two rules differ only for equal precedence.
  • Wrong: 8 - 3 - 2. The second - does not pop the first, so the output is 8 3 2 - -, which is 8 - (3 - 2) = 7 instead of 8 3 - 2 - = 3.
  • Why tests miss it: only an input with two operators of equal precedence in a row, where the operation does not associate (-, /), shows the difference. 2 + 3 + 4 gives a different postfix but the same value, so a test that checks only values passes.
  • > is right for a right-associative operator such as **: 2 ** 3 ** 2 means 2 ** (3 ** 2), so the later ** must wait on top of the earlier one.

essays.stem: Run the whole calculator on ( 8 - 2 ) / ( 1 + 2 ) * 4: convert it to postfix with the shunting-yard algorithm, then evaluate the postfix with a stack, showing the stack after each operator. Why is the answer a float?
essays.answer:
• Postfix: 8 2 - 1 2 + / 4 *. The )s output - and +; when * arrives, the / on the stack has equal precedence and leaves first.
  • Evaluation (stack bottom → top): - pops 2 and 8 → [6]; + pops 2 and 1 → [6, 3]; / pops 3 and 6 → [2.0]; * pops 4 and 2.0 → [8.0]. Exactly one value is left: the answer, 8.0.
  • A float because / is true division in Python: 6 / 3 is 2.0, and every result built on it stays a float.

essays.stem: Compare a stack on a dynamic array (top at the end) with a stack on a singly linked list (top at the head): the cost of push in the worst case and amortised, the memory per item, and memory locality. The lecture's timings found the linked stack faster in this course. Why, and would that still hold for Python's own list? Which would you choose for a program that must never pause?
essays.answer:
• Push: the array stack is amortised O(1), but a push that fills the block copies everything, O(n) for that one push. The linked stack is O(1) in the worst case: one node and one reference, every time.
  • Memory and locality: the array stores one reference per item (plus spare capacity) in one contiguous block; the linked stack needs a whole node per item (about 48 bytes), scattered in memory.
  • The measurement: every access to the course Array goes through a Python-level bounds check in dsa/array.py, while a node's next is a plain attribute. That is a constant factor, not a different Big-O. Python's own list, whose checks run in C, is faster than both.
  • Never pause: the linked stack, because its worst case is O(1) (or an array allocated once at its full size, so that it never resizes).

essays.stem: Design undo and redo for a text editor with two stacks. Say what each of action, Undo and Redo does to the two stacks, and show both stacks after: type A, type B, type C, undo, undo, redo, type D. What would go wrong if a new action did not clear the redo stack?
essays.answer:
• Action: push it on the undo stack and clear the redo stack. Undo: pop from undo, reverse it, push it on redo. Redo: pop from redo, do it again, push it on undo. Undo or Redo on an empty stack does nothing.
  • Trace: after A, B, C: undo [A, B, C], redo []. Undo, undo: undo [A], redo [C, B] (top B). Redo: undo [A, B], redo [C]. Type D: undo [A, B, D], redo [].
  • Without the clear, Redo would bring back C on top of D, an edit made to a different text, and the history would no longer describe a sequence of states the user actually saw.
